reading.body:
Energy is both an AI user and the binding constraint on AI scaling, with DOE quantifying datacenter power at 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and 6.7 to 12% projected by 2028.

The record splits into a shared research layer and deployment programs. DOE, EPRI, and IEEE PES track grid resilience, wildfire risk, asset health, and machine learning standards, while NextEra, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova, Baker Hughes, Halliburton, Shell, and ExxonMobil apply AI to renewable yield, digital twins, drilling, and seismic processing. Specialist firms Amperon, Grid4C, and Geoteric sell forecasting and subsurface mapping to utilities and energy desks.

For AI specifically, the pattern is circular: the sector that must supply power for datacenter compute is also using AI to optimize generation, batteries, and grid balancing. The data does not show whether those optimization gains are enough to offset the projected demand growth, nor does it quantify investment or performance across these programs.

summary: Grid optimisation, exploration, and the datacenter power crunch make energy both an AI user and AI's binding constraint. Who tracks it: the utility research bodies and DOE are the primary record, with the grid and oilfield incumbents' own technology programs layered on top.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use among utilities firms at 11.8% in the latest reading, down from 16.4% in the prior period. The survey covers Utilities under NAICS 22, and the Census Bureau notes that oil and gas extraction reports under mining rather than utilities, so the oilfield activity described by vendors below sits outside that figure. The measure itself is a narrow one: the share of firms answering yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks.

What the sources show being deployed splits into three areas. In forecasting, Amperon sells AI and machine learning software that produces load, price, and renewable forecasts for utilities, traders, and asset operators, drawing on 40,000 weather points from four vendors and about 25 weather variables analyzed hourly, with an ensemble model that blends forecasts from three weather vendors; the company says its models regularly beat ISOs and can forecast with up to 3x more accuracy. In exploration, Geoteric applies deep learning to 3D seismic data through its AI Hub, with modules for AI Data Conditioning, AI Geological Features, and AI Faults, and describes the technology as digitizing and decarbonizing upstream operations. In equipment and operations, Baker Hughes says its oilfield portfolio is enriched by digitalization, artificial intelligence, and automation capabilities that enable remote operations, reduce risk, and drive decarbonization, while its industrial solutions combine technology, data, and automation for asset, process, and sustainability performance.

The curated points name where vendors and operators concentrate. Siemens Energy and GE Vernova ship AI controllers and digital-twin software for gas, wind, and grid assets, so in that segment AI arrives as equipment rather than as a separate purchase. Baker Hughes and Halliburton deploy AI for autonomous drilling, reservoir simulation, and pipeline monitoring, and Shell and ExxonMobil run enterprise AI for seismic processing and predictive maintenance. NextEra Energy, described as the largest US renewable producer, forecasts wind and solar yield, optimizes battery dispatch, and automates plant maintenance with AI. Amperon and Grid4C are characterized as the specialist layer selling forecasting accuracy and smart-meter analytics to utilities and energy desks.

The research and standards layer is institutional. EPRI, the utility-backed Electric Power Research Institute, runs working groups on AI grid resilience, wildfire-risk prediction, and asset-health monitoring. IEEE PES publishes standards and research for machine learning in power systems, grid cyber-defense, and distributed energy resource management, and its technical committee working groups have produced over 900 IEEE Standards. The Department of Energy's Grid Modernization Initiative is described as the federal record of AI projects in real-time grid balancing, reactor optimization, and carbon capture across US utilities, and its Grid Modernization Laboratory Consortium provides technical assistance to the 7 US Independent System Operators and Regional Transmission Organizations.

The Department of Energy frames both the opportunity and the constraint. Its AI office describes the Genesis Mission, which combines DOE and National Lab supercomputing, scientific data, and AI capabilities into a single integrated system, and it notes that data centers are projected to consume up to 9% of total US electricity demand by 2030, with the largest growth dedicated to AI. DOE also launched the Speed to Power Initiative to accelerate large-scale grid infrastructure development and released the PermitAI tool for federal environmental permitting. On risk, DOE states that AI systems may generate incorrect, unverifiable, and potentially harmful outputs and that any use must properly understand and mitigate those risks. This site's Power and Cooling section cites DOE's 2024 LBNL report finding that datacenters consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023, projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, driven primarily by AI workloads, and reads that range as a hard constraint on AI scaling because the grid cannot expand as fast as compute demand grows.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few practical conclusions. The measured adoption figure is modest and moved down between periods, so this is not yet a sector where AI use is universal. The clearest vendor claims are about forecast accuracy and operational efficiency rather than cost savings, and the only quantified performance claims in these sources come from vendors describing their own products, such as Amperon's up to 3x more accurate forecasting and DOE's account of a 200x improvement in energy efficiency for high-performance computing achieved through the Exascale Computing Project. The regulatory posture visible here is federal and supportive rather than restrictive, with DOE running programs to speed power and permitting for AI datacenters while simultaneously warning about unverifiable outputs. The constraint a deployer should weigh is electricity: if datacenter demand moves toward the projected 6.7 to 12% of US consumption by 2028, the power and interconnection side of any energy AI plan may prove harder than the models.

https://amperon.co/.brief: Amperon states that its AI forecasting software provides load, price, and renewable forecasts for utilities, traders, and asset operators that are up to three times more accurate than existing solutions. The company attributes this to an AI/ML approach built for added complexity from renewables, batteries, and data centers. Its platform uses 40,000 weather points from four vendors and analyzes about 25 weather variables hourly, with an ensemble model blending forecasts from three vendors. Amperon was founded in 2018 by a former energy trader and data engineer with 15 years of industry experience, and the company says its model regularly beats ISOs.

https://ieee-pes.org/.brief: The IEEE Power and Energy Society describes itself as a nonprofit, member-driven organization that aims to be the foremost source of scientific and engineering knowledge about power and energy globally. The page states that its events are open to both members and non-members, with members receiving reduced registration fees, and that it publishes magazines, IEEE PES Transactions, and an open access journal. It reports that PES technical committee working groups have produced over 900 IEEE Standards and continue to generate nearly half of all IEEE Standards each year. The page also mentions a digital library called the IEEE PES Resource Center offering technical reports, presentations, and educational materials, along with opportunities to earn CEUs and PDHs. Active members receive complimentary subscriptions to IEEE Power & Energy and IEEE Electrification magazines, including a Spanish translation of the former.

https://www.epri.com/.brief: EPRI is a global research organization that uses science to support a reliable, affordable, and resilient energy future. Its mission is to benefit society, and it offers independent, objective thought leadership and industry expertise. EPRI works through a highly collaborative and rigorous approach.

https://www.energy.gov/ai.brief: The Department of Energy describes AI as technology that can make predictions, recommendations, or decisions by identifying patterns in data. DOE reports that it has sponsored foundational research in applied mathematics and computer science since the 1960s, and through initiatives like the Exascale Computing Project, achieved a 200x improvement in energy efficiency for high-performance computing while developing components now used in AI training chips. The department plans to build an integrated platform combining its computing power, scientific datasets, experimental facilities, and quantum computing to accelerate solutions to scientific and national-security problems, while also addressing the challenge that data centers are projected to consume up to 9 percent of total U.S. electricity by 2030. DOE acknowledges that "AI systems may generate incorrect, unverifiable, and potentially harmful outputs" and emphasizes the need to understand and mitigate these risks.

https://www.geoteric.com/.brief: Geoteric offers 3D seismic interpretation software for oil and gas that provides fast analysis to support exploration and production workflows. The company has introduced the Geoteric AI Hub, a new platform that lets geoscientists compare, contrast and experiment with different AI networks, parameters and scenarios in a modern, example-driven interface. Through the AI Hub, customers can use the latest modules, including AI Data Conditioning, AI Geological Features and AI Faults. The source reports that, building on more than three decades of subsurface technology experience, the software has been enhanced with first-to-market AI technology to achieve unprecedented, faster visualization of the subsurface, and it says “Geoteric AI is revolutionizing our upstream exploration efforts.”

https://www.nexteraenergy.com/.brief: NextEra Energy says it is merging with Dominion Energy to strengthen supply in four fast-growing states while keeping power affordable. The company reports that Florida Power & Light serves more than 6 million accounts, powering roughly 12 million Floridians. It also claims to have the largest and most diverse portfolio of power generation and infrastructure solutions, spanning renewables, storage, natural gas and nuclear. Additionally, NextEra Energy notes that over 17 000 employees volunteer in community and animal-care activities.

https://www.siemens-energy.com/.brief: Siemens Energy says it supports companies and countries in cutting emissions across the energy landscape to create a more reliable, affordable and sustainable system. The company claims to be a leader in energy technology, helping worldwide firms and nations build resilient, affordable and sustainable energy systems. Siemens Energy reports that it is preparing to spin off its Transformation of Industry business area into a standalone company. In its Q3 FY 2026 earnings release, Siemens Energy says it has “accelerated profitable growth”, with Siemens Gamesa reporting a positive quarterly result, and it also says it is preparing to launch an independent brand.

https://www.energy.gov/gmi/grid-moderniz.brief: The Grid Modernization Initiative (GMI) is a Department of Energy program that partners with industry to develop advanced grid technologies. It aims to create a “modern grid of the future” by working with public and private partners to develop tools that measure, analyze, predict, protect, and control the grid, addressing the current grid’s lack of 21st-century attributes. GMI’s portfolio focuses on integrating all electricity sources, improving grid security, solving energy-storage and distributed-generation challenges, and providing a platform for U.S. competitiveness. The initiative also co-sponsored the 2024 Energy Transition Summit and established a collaboration through the Grid Modernization Laboratory Consortium to offer technical assistance to seven independent system operators and regional transmission organizations.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: According to the Department of Energy's 2024 analysis, datacenter electricity consumption in the US rose from 4.4% in 2023 and is projected to reach between 6.7% and 12% by 2028, with AI workloads as the primary driver. This growth trajectory represents a fundamental constraint on AI scaling, since electricity grid expansion cannot keep pace with rising compute demand. Meeting even modest AI training and inference needs at scale will require new generation capacity, storage infrastructure, or load-shifting capabilities that do not yet exist, and the wide projection range reflects uncertainty about actual AI deployment speed.
